key_insight: Not all deviations of proxy rewards from ground truth are harmful: some classes of reward errors can actually help policy-gradient training by directing probability mass toward better outputs. The paper categorizes these imperfect rewards and shows theoretically which outputs attract probability under policy gradient.
problem_solved: Addresses the gap that standard reward-quality metrics (e.g., ranking accuracy) treat all reward errors as equally bad, failing to predict when imperfect proxy rewards will help or hurt policy-gradient optimization.
method: Theoretical analysis of policy-gradient dynamics to determine which outputs gain probability mass under imperfect rewards.
Formal categorization of reward errors (e.g., beneficial, neutral, harmful) based on their impact on optimization trajectories.
Propose criteria/metrics beyond ranking accuracy and validate insights with illustrative simulations/experiments on language-model tasks.
impact: Provides practitioners principled guidance for designing and evaluating proxy rewards (e.g., in RLHF), enabling more robust training by distinguishing harmless or helpful reward errors from truly harmful ones.
visual_elements: Taxonomy diagram showing reward-error categories (Beneficial | Neutral | Harmful) with brief examples
Flow diagram of policy-gradient dynamics illustrating which outputs attract probability under each error type
Comparative bar/line chart: traditional ranking-accuracy vs. proposed criteria in predicting training outcomes
Toy reward landscape + policy update arrows to visualize how certain errors steer optimization toward better or worse outputs
paper_title: When Errors Can Be Beneficial: A Categorization of Imperfect Rewards for Policy Gradient
paper_authors: Shuning Shang, Hubert Strauss, Stanley Wei, Sanjeev Arora, Noam Razin
